items.text: The double empathy problem isn't really about empathy. It's about whose emotional style gets to count as 'normal' — and whose gets pathologised for not matching it.
items.rationale: Upgrades a concept the community already knows into something sharper — naming structural injustice rather than individual misunderstanding. Recognition plus reframe in one move, directly supported by the 2026 Tandfonline paper.

items.text: Half-understood in autistic spaces, half-understood in ADHD spaces — that's not you being too complicated. That's you having a neurotype the system hadn't built a word for yet.
items.rationale: Names the AuDHD liminal experience a fast-growing community has described for years without clinical language. 'Many' and 'you' framing keeps it appropriately scoped; high recognition, no exaggeration.

items.text: Autistic burnout isn't a motivation problem. It's a capacity problem. When demand exceeds capacity, the nervous system stops the output. That's not giving up. That's how nervous systems work.
items.rationale: Directly counters the 'lazy/no willpower' read that late-diagnosed autistic adults carry longest. Clinical enough to feel grounded without making a diagnostic claim. Phrasing is tight and quotable.

items.text: Rest alone doesn't fix autistic burnout. You also have to reduce load. The nervous system can't recover while the demand that caused the crash is still in place.
items.rationale: Practical sub-point that stands fully alone. Useful, not preachy. The 'rest isn't enough' claim is directly drawn from the linked source and adds something genuinely actionable.

items.text: Many autistic people coped — until university. Or a new baby. Or a bereavement. These aren't random breakdowns. They're predictable moments where compensation hits its limit.
items.rationale: Names the shape of late-diagnosis stories. Reduces self-blame for 'why now?' without requiring anyone to justify themselves. 'Many' is appropriately scoped; the examples are concrete without being prescriptive.

items.text: Late-diagnosis grief isn't one undifferentiated fog. It's specific: the younger self who thought they were broken. The friendships that didn't survive burnout. The paths never offered.
items.rationale: Reframes grief as plural and specific rather than vague — which is both more accurate and more workable. The list structure earns its length; each item will hit differently for different readers.

items.text: For a PDA-profile nervous system, a demand registers as a threat to safety or autonomy. 'Just comply' isn't available — the same way 'just calm down' isn't during a fire alarm. That's wiring, not defiance.
items.rationale: Gives parents and PDA adults a reframe that is both visceral and clean. The fire alarm analogy communicates involuntary nature without requiring the reader to know the clinical literature.
items.sensitivity_flag: PDA is not universally recognised as a standalone clinical category; 'PDA-profile' language is appropriate but this framing sits within neurodiversity-affirming practice rather than mainstream diagnostic consensus — worth knowing before quoting it in clinical contexts.

items.text: Low-demand parenting isn't 'no rules.' It's asking 'is this genuinely necessary?' before anything gets added to the pile. The non-negotiables stay. Everything else gets triaged.
items.rationale: Addresses parent guilt directly by drawing the distinction between low-demand and permissive in terms any sceptical relative could actually hear. Crisp, usable, and sourced to Amanda Diekman's explicit framing.

items.text: Needing co-regulation to return to baseline isn't immaturity. For many autistic nervous systems, that's how regulation works. Self-regulation is the outcome — not the prerequisite.
items.rationale: Counters shame around needing external support to regulate. 'Many' appropriately scopes the claim. Practically useful and emotionally validating without being prescriptive or implying this is universal.

items.text: What actually helps your nervous system land? Not what's supposed to work — what does, for you.
items.rationale: Opens a genuine discussion rather than collecting passive likes. Deliberately short. No correct answer implied; invites the audience to share lived strategies without any prescriptive framing from the post itself.

items.text: Neurodivergent accommodations are now the third most common reason Gen Z employees ask HR for help. The question has shifted from 'can I ask for this' to 'what happens when I do.'
items.rationale: Grounds a real structural shift in a concrete stat without overselling it. The second sentence adds genuine tension that invites engagement from people who've had both good and bad experiences at work.
items.sensitivity_flag: Stat is drawn from a single 2026 HR industry survey, not peer-reviewed research. Accurately reported per the briefing, but should not be presented as settled population-level data if quoted elsewhere.

items.text: If you were diagnosed late, which loss hit hardest? Not 'the years' in general — the specific thing. The friendship. The degree. The version of yourself you couldn't be.
items.rationale: Takes the specific-grief insight from Angle 5 and turns it into a discussion opener that earns replies rather than just affirmations. Invites people to name something real; the examples model the specificity without limiting it.
